newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's new government signals tough line on EMU.
newsitem.headline: France's new government signals tough line on EMU.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government is showing it can stick to its electoral promises, defying cynics who predicted otherwise.

Despite furious spin intended to reassure financial markets, French and German leaders were forced on Friday to admit they had been unable to resolve a dispute on a planned budgetary discipline pact that would underpin European monetary union.

The failure forced the two sides at the Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France, into extended talks this weekend to try to hammer out an accord on the "stability pact" ahead of an EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.

The German-inspired pact, which would impose tough sanctions on countries that stray from budgetary discipline once the single currency is launched in 1999, was agreed in Dublin last December and was due for ratification in Amsterdam.

Abiding by an election pledge to reorient the drive to European monetary union, French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin refused to back down from demands that Europe's single currency plans take Europe's 18 million jobless into account.
Jospin said France supported launching the "euro" on schedule but wanted a fundamentally different approach to European construction.
"Other considerations exist (aside from budgetary discipline)," he said. "These considerations touching on jobs, growth and economic cooperation are equally very important."

France, a French government source said, was seeking a European jobs and growth pact that would have the same weight as the stability pact. Germany has insisted that it would not back any measures which would require fund transfers to Brussels.

During the election campaign which ended with their stunning victory on June 1 over the centre-right coalition, the Socialists pledged to seek to put economic growth and jobs at the top of Europe's political agenda.
Economists say the unusual spectacle of a government living up to its campaign promises should come as no surprise in this instance.

They say the Socialists, mindful of how ruthlessly voters turned on the previous centre-right government for not honouring its campaign pledges, had to respect at least part of their platform. "Their political survival is linked to this," said Credit Agricole Indosuez economist Arnaud Mares.

Juergen Pfister, economist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt said that given the decisive change in the French political landscape, "any continuation of financial policies of the old government can be practically ruled out now."
"If they did, it would be a complete rupture of their election promises," he said.

A French source conceded the problems when he said President Jacques Chirac, forced by his centre-right coalition's defeat to share power with the left, told German Chancellor Helmut Kohl the election had raised expectations which could make it tougher to meet Maastricht treaty conditions for a single currency.
Both France and Germany were anxious to play down any talk of a rift between Paris and Bonn, whose alliance is regarded as crucial to pushing monetary union through in 1999.
But economists said despite upbeat talk from both sides, an agreement at Amsterdam was far from certain.
"It's not impossible, but it is far from being a done deal," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said, adding that he "had the impression Jospin was not going to bend."

"There was nothing in anything (French Finance Minister Dominique) Strauss-Kahn or Jospin said that suggests they are going to soften their position. They are sticking to their guns," Iain Lindsay, bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said.
